column1: Reconstruct Argument 1: Sense is motion, the materialist account of perception (Lev. 1; Third Objections).
column2:
Aim: perception is a chain of motions from object to brain and heart; the colors and sounds we perceive are not in objects as they appear; the schoolmen's species do not exist.
Premises: every thought begins in sense, "there is no conception in a mans mind, which hath not at first, totally, or by parts, been begotten upon the organs of Sense" (Lev. 1.2); an external body presses the organ, the pressure goes by the nerves to brain and heart, and the heart's outward endeavour "seemeth to be some matter without" (Lev. 1.4); only motion is present at each stage, "for motion, produceth nothing but motion" (Lev. 1.4); appearances can be separated from objects (mirrors, echoes).
Conclusion: "Sense in all cases, is nothing els but originall fancy" (Lev. 1.4); imagination is "nothing but Decaying Sense" (Lev. 2.2).
Objection: if seeming is a motion, why does this motion seem a red patch out there? If it is not, motion has produced something other than motion. Descartes: motion and spirit are of two entirely different kinds (the gap Leibniz's mill and Levine later sharpened).
Reply (the literature's): Hobbes identifies appearing with the body's own motion, as imagination and memory are one decaying motion (Lev. 2.3), so the question is for physiology. The debt remains: he says that sense is motion, never how a motion appears. Open.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 2: Reasoning is reckoning, names, definitions and truth in speech (Lev. 4-5).
column2:
Aim: reasoning is adding and subtracting names; truth belongs to speech, not things; science is knowledge of the consequences of definitions.
Premises: names are arbitrary marks, and there is "nothing in the world Universall but Names" (Lev. 4.6); "True and False are attributes of Speech, not of things" (Lev. 4.11); so a reasoner must first fix definitions, as geometers do, since "words are wise mens counters" (Lev. 4.13); a name joining inconsistent names, such as "Incorporeall Body", signifies nothing (Lev. 4.22); reason is "nothing but Reckoning (that is, Adding and Substracting) of the Consequences of generall names agreed upon" (Lev. 5.2); no one's reason is the certain reason, so disputants must set up an arbitrator (Lev. 5.3).
Conclusion: science is conditional knowledge of what follows from agreed names; where reckoners disagree there is no natural umpire, only an appointed one (the shape of the sovereign).
Objection: Descartes: in reasoning we unite the things signified, not names; Leibniz: this makes truth depend on arbitrary definitions; and the incorporeal-substance step assumes the materialism at issue.
Reply: the names are arbitrary but their consequences are not, so reckoning is not arbitrary; the chapter 4 point on incorporeal substance does beg the question, and Hobbes's better argument is elsewhere (De Corpore; Lev. 46.15). Open.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 3: Against the thinking substance, the Third Objections on the cogito (Obj. III, Obj. 2).
column2:
Aim: the cogito shows that a thinking something exists, not what kind of thing it is; if anything, what thinks is a body.
Premises: "I am a thing that thinks; quite correct" (Obj. III, Obj. 2); but "I am exercising thought, hence I am thought" is no better than "I am walking; hence I am the walking" (Obj. III, Obj. 2); we distinguish a subject from its activities and can conceive subjects of activity only bodily, "as in material guise" (Obj. III, Obj. 2); the wax is the same matter under changing qualities.
Conclusion: "the proper inference seems to be that that which thinks is material rather than immaterial" (Obj. III, Obj. 2).
Objection: Descartes: by mind he meant what has the faculty of thinking, not the faculty; he left the question "wholly undetermined until Meditation VI" (Obj. III, reply to Obj. 2); and acts of thought have no affinity with corporeal acts.
Reply (the literature's): this concedes Hobbes's point that the cogito alone proves no immaterial mind, so all weight falls on Meditation VI; Hobbes answers that elsewhere (De Corpore 3.4: conceiving thought apart from body does not show it can exist apart). Descartes's counter: clear and distinct conceivability. Open.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 4: The restless desire of power after power (Lev. 6, 10, 11).
column2:
Aim: a general inclination of all mankind to seek power after power, which follows from what desire is, not from special greed.
Premises: voluntary motion begins in endeavour; endeavour toward is appetite (Lev. 6.2); good is relative: the words are "ever used with relation to the person that useth them" (Lev. 6.7); there is no final end, "Felicity is a continuall progresse of the desire, from one object to another" (Lev. 11.1); power is a man's "present means, to obtain some future apparent Good" (Lev. 10.1) and is comparative.
Conclusion: "a perpetuall and restlesse desire of Power after power, that ceaseth onely in Death" (Lev. 11.2), because "he cannot assure the power and means to live well, which he hath present, without the acquisition of more" (Lev. 11.2).
Objection: it slanders human nature (Clarendon; the moral-sense writers) and reduces motives to self-interest; Lev. 11.4–5 itself says desire of ease and fear of death dispose men to obey.
Reply: the moderate are drawn in by the immoderate (Lev. 13.4); the desire is a response to insecurity, not greed, and needs no egoism. Open: Strauss (vanity), Macpherson (market society), Gert against Kavka on egoism.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 5: Natural equality (Lev. 13).
column2:
Aim: people are equal by nature in the one sense the politics needs, so no one can claim by nature a benefit another may not claim, and all hope equally to attain their ends.
Premises: "the difference between man, and man, is not so considerable, as that one man can thereupon claim to himselfe any benefit, to which another may not pretend, as well as he" (Lev. 13.1); "the weakest has strength enough to kill the strongest" (Lev. 13.1), by plot or confederacy; in mind, "Prudence, is but Experience" and equal time gives it equally (Lev. 13.2).
Conclusion: "From this equality of ability, ariseth equality of hope in the attaining of our Ends" (Lev. 13.3).
Objection: false as equal ability, irrelevant as equal vulnerability; and confederacies mean the primitive units are groups, not equals.
Reply: only rough equality is needed, enough that no one can count on dominating; groups are as dangerous as individuals; and the ninth law makes the point practical, since those who think themselves equal will accept peace only on equal terms. Hoekstra reads the claim as partly a political recommendation. Open.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 6: The state of nature is a war of all against all, the three causes of quarrel (Lev. 13).
column2:
Aim: wherever there is no common power to overawe all, there is a condition of war of every man against every man, and life there is miserable.
Premises: equal hope makes rivals enemies; distrust makes anticipation the reasonable course (Lev. 13.4); some enjoy conquest and the rest must keep pace; each demands esteem. "three principall causes of quarrel. First, Competition; Secondly, Diffidence; Thirdly, Glory" (Lev. 13.6). War is a known disposition to fight, not constant battle, as foul weather is "an inclination thereto of many dayes together" (Lev. 13.8).
Conclusion: without a common power men are in "that condition which is called Warre; and such a warre, as is of every man, against every man" (Lev. 13.8), the life of man "solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short" (Lev. 13.9); "Where there is no common Power, there is no Law: where no Law, no Injustice" (Lev. 13.13).
Objection: there was never such a condition; it projects socialized vanity; Hampton's dilemma: if the war comes from passion it survives the contract, if from rationality the contract will not be kept.
Reply: Hobbes grants it was "never generally so, over all the world" (Lev. 13.11) and says civil war shows it; Kavka: rational anticipation plus some vain passions plus disagreement in judgment, which the sovereign changes by changing the situation, not human nature. Open (rationality, passions or judgment).

column1: Reconstruct Argument 7: The right of nature and the first law of nature (Lev. 14).
column2:
Aim: each person has a right to do whatever they judge necessary for their life, which leaves everyone insecure, so reason delivers a rule: seek peace where it can be had, defend yourself where it cannot.
Premises: the right of nature is "the Liberty each man hath, to use his own power, as he will himselfe, for the preservation of his own Nature" (Lev. 14.1); liberty is "the absence of externall Impediments" (Lev. 14.2); a law of nature is "a Precept, or generall Rule, found out by Reason" forbidding what destroys life (Lev. 14.3); right and law "differ as much, as Obligation, and Liberty" (Lev. 14.3); in war "every man has a Right to every thing; even to one anothers body" (Lev. 14.4).
Conclusion: first law, "To seek Peace, and follow it", with the right of defense as its second branch (Lev. 14.5).
Objection: a right to everything that binds no one is empty; and a precept of reason about one's life is prudence, not law.
Reply: the emptiness is Hobbes's point, since it gives reason its motive for peace; the laws are also God's word, so "properly called Lawes" (Lev. 15.41), which is Argument 10's dispute. Open: Taylor and Warrender (divine command), Nagel and Gauthier (prudence), Lloyd (reciprocity).

column1: Reconstruct Argument 8: Laying down rights, covenants, and the rights no one can give up (Lev. 14).
column2:
Aim: reason requires each to lay down the right to all things if others do; a right is laid down by a voluntary sign; covenants of mutual trust are void in nature on reasonable suspicion but bind under a power; some rights cannot be given up.
Premises: the second law says to be willing, when others are, "to lay down this right to all things" (Lev. 14.6), since to do it alone is "to expose himselfe to Prey" (Lev. 14.6); laying down a right removes an impediment and obliges one not to hinder the beneficiary, and doing so is injustice; but "of the voluntary acts of every man, the object is some Good To Himselfe" (Lev. 14.9), so the right to resist force against one's life cannot be transferred; "the bonds of words are too weak to bridle mens ambition, avarice, anger, and other Passions, without the feare of some coerceive Power" (Lev. 14.19).
Conclusion: contract needs a common power; "A Covenant not to defend my selfe from force, by force, is alwayes voyd" (Lev. 14.30).
Objection: assurance (how is the founding covenant made?); injustice as absurdity confuses logic with action; the retained right undermines absolutism (Bramhall's charge that the book is a rebel's catechism).
Reply: the founding covenant is made all at once with a power; fear that voids a covenant must arise after it; the retained right is narrow and defensive (Sreedhar). Open (Hampton: alienation or agency).

column1: Reconstruct Argument 9: The reply to the Fool (Lev. 15).
column2:
Aim: keeping a valid covenant is never against reason, even for someone who cares only for their own preservation, so justice is a law of nature and not a useful name.
Premises: the Fool says "there is no such thing as Justice" and that breach "was not against Reason, when it conduced to ones benefit" (Lev. 15.4); the case is the second performer, after the other side has performed or where a power compels both; reason judges by what can be foreseen, not by luck; in war no one can defend himself without allies; a breaker declares that he thinks breach reasonable, so he "cannot be received into any Society, that unite themselves for Peace and defence, but by the errour of them that receive him" (Lev. 15.5); other men's errors cannot reasonably be counted on.
Conclusion: "Justice therefore, that is to say, Keeping of Covenant, is a Rule of Reason, by which we are forbidden to do any thing destructive to our life; and consequently a Law of Nature" (Lev. 15.7).
Objection: it works only against the careless knave; the clever Fool breaks faith only when breach stays secret (Hume's sensible knave); Hampton: if agents can keep covenants, the war of nature does not follow, and if not, they cannot found the sovereign.
Reply (the literature's): Kavka: when the possible loss is catastrophic and detection is hard to estimate, the prudent rule is to keep covenants; Gauthier: the constrained maximizer does better; the reply covers only second performers, and the sovereign turns every covenant into that case. Open (Hoekstra, Lloyd).

column1: Reconstruct Argument 10: Laws of nature as theorems, are they laws, and whose? (Lev. 15 end; Lev. 26).
column2:
Aim: the laws of nature are conclusions of reason about self-preservation, and are laws properly only as commanded, by God or by the civil sovereign; which source finally obliges is the open question.
Premises: law properly is command, "the word of him, that by right hath command over others" (Lev. 15.41); the dictates of reason are "but Conclusions, or Theoremes concerning what conduceth to the conservation and defence of themselves" (Lev. 15.41), so called laws only improperly; considered as God's word they are properly laws; in a commonwealth the sovereign commands them too; the laws "oblige In Foro Interno" but not always in action, since keeping them alone would make one "a prey to others" (Lev. 15.36).
Conclusion: "The Law of Nature, and the Civill Law, contain each other, and are of equall extent" (Lev. 26).
Objection: Cumberland: Hobbes reduces law to advice and buys it back with one sentence about God; from the other side, if God's right rests on power, obligation is only prudence toward the strong.
Reply (the literature's): prudential readers accept the second horn as hypothetical imperatives; theological readers point to Lev. 31 and Hobbes's vocabulary of sin; Lloyd derives them from reciprocity. Open: Taylor and Warrender, Hood and Martinich against Nagel, Watkins and Gauthier.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 11: Authorization, persons, actors and the representative (Lev. 16-17).
column2:
Aim: a multitude becomes one person, the commonwealth, only by each authorizing one representative, so that the representative's acts count as the acts of each of them.
Premises: an artificial person's words represent another, and where the one represented owns them, "the Person is the Actor; and he that owneth his words and actions, is the AUTHOR" (Lev. 16); authority is a right to act, and what the actor does within it binds the author; "it is the Unity of the Representer, not the Unity of the Represented, that maketh the Person One" (Lev. 16); each member authorizes: "I Authorise and give up my Right of Governing my selfe, to this Man, or to this Assembly of men, on this condition, that thou give up thy Right to him, and Authorise all his Actions in like manner" (Lev. 17).
Conclusion: the commonwealth is "One Person, of whose Acts a great Multitude, by mutuall Covenants one with another, have made themselves every one the Author" (Lev. 17); so a subject cannot be injured by what the sovereign does.
Objection: authorizing everything makes subjects share responsibility for everything, yet Lev. 42 makes obedient acts the sovereign's; Filmer: no one ever assembled to authorize; Hampton: agency, not alienation.
Reply: Hobbes needs no assembly (acquisition, Argument 13); authorization is ownership as a matter of right, not moral blame (Lloyd). Open: Skinner (the state as person), Chwaszcza, Martinich.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 12: Sovereignty must be absolute and undivided (Lev. 18, 29).
column2:
Aim: whoever holds sovereignty must hold all its essential rights together and be subject to no lawful check by subjects, courts or rival bodies; divided sovereignty causes civil war.
Premises: the covenant is among the subjects, so the sovereign cannot breach it; any condition on the sovereign needs a judge, and "there is in this case, no Judge to decide the controversie: it returns therefore to the Sword again" (Lev. 18); "Covenants being but words, and breath, have no force to oblige, contain, constrain, or protect any man, but what it has from the publique Sword" (Lev. 18); the essential rights depend on one another, and are "incommunicable, and inseparable" (Lev. 18); divided powers make rival representatives.
Conclusion: "what is it to divide the Power of a Common-wealth, but to Dissolve it; for Powers divided mutually destroy each other" (Lev. 29).
Objection: Locke: it is folly to guard against polecats and foxes yet be devoured by lions; and divided constitutions have been stable (Kavka: the premises support a strong, not an absolute, sovereign).
Reply: "the estate of Man can never be without some incommodity or other" (Lev. 18), and the harm is slight beside civil war; the claim is about final authority, not division of labor. Open: Hampton, Kavka, Sommerville, Tuck.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 13: Commonwealth by acquisition, covenants made in fear bind (Lev. 14, 20).
column2:
Aim: a conqueror who spares the vanquished in exchange for submission gets the rights of a sovereign by institution, because covenants made in fear are valid and every commonwealth rests on fear.
Premises: "Covenants entred into by fear, in the condition of meer Nature, are obligatory" (Lev. 14); a fearful act is still voluntary (Lev. 21.3); acquisition differs from institution "onely in this, That men who choose their Soveraign, do it for fear of one another, and not of him whom they Institute" (Lev. 20); to deny that fear binds is to say "no man, in any kind of Common-wealth, could be obliged to Obedience" (Lev. 20).
Conclusion: "It is not therefore the Victory, that giveth the right of Dominion over the Vanquished, but his own Covenant" (Lev. 20), so "the Rights, and Consequences of Soveraignty, are the same in both" (Lev. 20). A captive in chains has made no covenant and owes nothing.
Objection: this makes might into right (Locke on conquest; Clarendon on Cromwell), and a coerced promise is no consent.
Reply: the right comes from the subject's own act, not from victory; civil law can discharge extorted promises; and a theory that voids fear-based covenants condemns every commonwealth. Open: Skinner and Hoekstra on the de facto turn; Hampton against Lloyd and Sreedhar.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 14: The liberty of subjects and the right to resist (Lev. 21).
column2:
Aim: the liberty of subjects does not limit the sovereign, yet every subject keeps liberties no covenant can transfer, above all to resist those who would kill or wound him.
Premises: "Liberty, or FREEDOME, signifieth (properly) the absence of Opposition" (Lev. 21.1); laws are artificial chains, and "in all kinds of actions, by the laws praetermitted, men have the Liberty, of doing what their own reasons shall suggest, for the most profitable to themselves" (Lev. 21.6); this is no limit on the sovereign, since each subject is author of his acts (Lev. 21.7); but "Covenants, not to defend a mans own body, are voyd" (Lev. 21.11).
Conclusion: a man ordered to kill or wound himself, "though justly condemned", "yet hath that man the Liberty to disobey" (Lev. 21.12); and "The Obligation of Subjects to the Soveraign is understood to last as long, and no longer, than the power lasteth, by which he is able to protect them" (Lev. 21.21).
Objection: if each subject judges when his life is threatened and when protection fails, the state of nature was never left (Bramhall; Hampton's dilemma).
Reply: the liberty is individual and defensive, not a public right to judge the sovereign, and no one may help the resister (Lev. 21.17); Sreedhar: it is consistent with absolutism. Open: Hampton, Sreedhar, Curran, Skinner on republican liberty.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 15: The civil sovereign governs religion (Lev. 12, 32-33, 39, 42).
column2:
Aim: in a Christian commonwealth no church has authority of its own against the state; the sovereign settles the canon, the preaching and the public profession, and only inward belief lies beyond his reach.
Premises: sovereignty is undivided, so a "Ghostly Authority" against the civil one is a disease (Lev. 29); a church able to command is the same thing as a Christian commonwealth, for "Temporall and Spirituall Government, are but two words brought into the world, to make men see double, and mistake their Lawfull Soveraign" (Lev. 39); "those Books only are Canonicall, that is, Law, in every nation, which are established for such by the Soveraign Authority" (Lev. 33); "Beleef, and Unbeleef never follow mens Commands" (Lev. 42); a compelled profession is the sovereign's act (Naaman); the one necessary article is "that JESUS IS THE CHRIST" (Lev. 43).
Conclusion: "the Civill Soveraign is the Supreme Pastor, to whose charge the whole flock of his Subjects is committed" (Lev. 42).
Objection: God must be obeyed rather than men (Bellarmine; Presbyterians), the martyrs died for nothing; and the argument is an insincere attack on revealed religion.
Reply: under a Christian sovereign nothing necessary conflicts; under an infidel one, faith stays inward and martyrdom remains, rebellion does not (Lev. 43); his late corporeal God is odd theism, not atheism (SEP). Open: Martinich against Curley, Strauss and Jesseph; toleration (Ryan, Collins against Sommerville).

column1: Reconstruct Argument 16: Liberty and necessity, Hobbes's compatibilism against Bramhall (Lev. 21; Of Liberty and Necessity).
column2:
Aim: every action is necessitated by prior causes, and this takes nothing from liberty rightly defined or from the justice of laws, praise and punishment.
Premises: "I acknowledge this liberty, that I can do if I will; but to say, I can will if I will, I take to be an absurd speech" (LN, EW IV 240); liberty is "the absence of all the impediments to action that are not contained in the nature and intrinsical quality of the agent" (LN, EW IV 273); the will is the last appetite in deliberation; nothing begins from itself, so "the cause of his will, is not the will itself, but something else not in his own disposing" (LN, EW IV 274); a sufficient cause is a necessary cause, so "whatsoever is produced, is produced necessarily" (LN, EW IV 275).
Conclusion: "Liberty and Necessity are Consistent" (Lev. 21.4).
Objection: Bramhall: "but real necessity and true liberty can never meet together" (Questions, No. III, EW V); necessity makes laws unjust, deliberation vain, punishment pointless, and God the author of sin. Modern form: freedom needs the ability to do otherwise.
Reply: "it is the consultation that causeth a man, and necessitateth him to choose to do one thing rather than another" (LN, EW IV 254); punishment and praise shape wills, so necessity works through them. Open: McKenna's compulsion objection; Jackson, Skinner on the context.

column1: Explain endeavour in Hobbes's sense and say what appetite and aversion are (Lev. 6.1–2).
column2:
Endeavour is the smallest beginning of motion inside the body, before any visible act: "These small beginnings of Motion, within the body of Man, before they appear in walking, speaking, striking, and other visible actions, are commonly called ENDEAVOUR" (Lev. 6.1).
Directed toward its cause it is appetite or desire: "when it is toward something which causes it, is called APPETITE, or DESIRE" (Lev. 6.2); directed away it is aversion.
Why it matters: the passions become mechanics, so the theory of action is part of physics; smallness of a motion is no argument against its existence.

column1: Explain Hobbes's account of good and evil and the political problem it creates (Lev. 6.7).
column2:
Good and evil name appetite and aversion: "that is it, which he for his part calleth Good" (Lev. 6.7). There is no "common Rule of Good and evill, to be taken from the nature of the objects themselves" (Lev. 6.7).
Where a common rule can come from: in a commonwealth, the person who represents it; elsewhere, an arbitrator the disputants agree on (Lev. 6.7, paraphrased).
So the theory of value and the theory of sovereignty meet: appetites differ between people and over time, and only a public judge can supply a common measure.

column1: Explain deliberation and the will, and say what follows for free will (Lev. 6.49–53).
column2:
Deliberation is the alternating of appetites, aversions, hopes and fears about one action: "the whole sum of Desires, Aversions, Hopes and Feares, continued till the thing be either done, or thought impossible, is that we call DELIBERATION" (Lev. 6.49).
The will is its end point: "Will, therefore, Is The Last Appetite In Deliberating" (Lev. 6.53); the act, not a faculty. Beasts deliberate too.
Consequences: the will is caused like any appetite, so freedom cannot be freedom of the will from causes (Argument 16); acts done from fear are voluntary, so covenants made in fear can bind (Argument 13).

column1: Explain felicity in Hobbes and say whom it opposes (Lev. 6.58; 11.1).
column2:
Felicity is success, not rest: "Continual Successe in obtaining those things which a man from time to time desireth, that is to say, continual prospering, is that men call FELICITY" (Lev. 6.58).
There is no highest good at which desire stops, and "Felicity is a continuall progresse of the desire, from one object to another" (Lev. 11.1).
It opposes the old moral philosophers' Summum Bonum and, in particular, Aquinas's single last end of every will. With no shared final end, nothing in nature lets a community be built on a common good; the commonwealth must be built another way.

column1: Define power and worth in Hobbes and say why power is comparative (Lev. 10).
column2:
Power is a man's "present means, to obtain some future apparent Good" (Lev. 10.1), either original (strength, prudence, eloquence) or instrumental (riches, reputation, friends, luck).
Worth is a market value: "his Price; that is to say, so much as would be given for the use of his Power" (Lev. 10.16), so it depends on others' need and judgment. Reputation of power is power.
Because others' power can block mine, security needs a margin over theirs, which feeds the restless desire of power after power (Argument 4).

column1: State the resolutive-compositive method and show how it fits the state of nature (De Cive Preface).
column2:
Knowledge is of effects from causes. Resolution takes a confusedly known whole apart to its causes; composition puts it back together from causes you understand. The model is the watch, taken apart and viewed in parts.
For the state, the Preface to De Cive asks us not to take states apart but to consider them "as if they were dissolved" (De Cive Preface, Molesworth II). It is not a historical claim: Hobbes does not say he saw states fall apart.
So: the state of nature is resolution (human nature with the common power thought away); covenant and sovereign are composition. Open question: whether he took the method from Zabarella, Galileo or the geometers.

column1: Explain why Hobbes holds that incorporeal substance is a contradiction (Lev. 34.2; 46.15).
column2:
Everything that exists is body, and every change is motion. "Substance and Body, signifie the same thing; and therefore Substance Incorporeall are words, which when they are joined together, destroy one another" (Lev. 34.2).
Universe: "every part of the Universe, is Body" (Lev. 46.15), and what is no part of it is Nothing; so a word for a thing that is no body names nothing.
It is a thesis about meaning as well as physics (compare "Round Quadrangle", Lev. 4.22). Spirits in Scripture are read as thin invisible bodies. Open: whether the late corporeal God is a heterodox theism or disguised atheism.

column1: Distinguish science from prudence in Hobbes (Lev. 3.7; 5.17).
column2:
Science is conditional knowledge of consequences: "Science is the knowledge of Consequences, and dependance of one fact upon another" (Lev. 5.17), reckoned from agreed definitions.
Prudence is foresight from experience, never certain: "it be called Prudence, when the Event answereth our Expectation; yet in its own nature, it is but Presumption" (Lev. 3.7); the more experience, the more prudent.
Link to politics: Hobbes's civil science claims the first kind of knowledge, while the equality argument (Lev. 13.2) rests on prudence being experience that equal time gives equally.

column1: State Hobbes's principle of inertia and the scholastic view it is aimed at (Lev. 2.1).
column2:
That when a thing lies still, unlesse somewhat els stirre it, it will lye still for ever, is a truth that no man doubts of (Lev. 2.1); by the same reason a thing in motion stays in motion unless something stops it.
Target: the scholastics, who said heavy bodies fall out of an appetite to rest, ascribing appetite to inanimate things.
Role: nothing moves itself, so every motion has a prior contiguous cause, which grounds the causal chain behind sense, appetite and, in Of Liberty and Necessity, the claim that the will too is caused.

column1: Define the right of nature and say what kind of right it is (Lev. 14.1).
column2:
The RIGHT OF NATURE, which Writers commonly call Jus Naturale, is the Liberty each man hath, to use his own power, as he will himselfe, for the preservation of his own Nature; that is to say, of his own Life (Lev. 14.1).
A right here is a liberty, the absence of an obligation, not a claim that others must respect; so two people can each have a right to the same thing.
With the condition of war it yields "every man has a Right to every thing; even to one anothers body" (Lev. 14.4), which gives no security and so motivates peace.

column1: Define a law of nature and say how it differs from a right (Lev. 14.3; 15.41).
column2:
A LAW OF NATURE, (Lex Naturalis,) is a Precept, or generall Rule, found out by Reason, by which a man is forbidden to do, that, which is destructive of his life, or taketh away the means of preserving the same (Lev. 14.3).
Right and law "differ as much, as Obligation, and Liberty" (Lev. 14.3): right is liberty to do or forbear, law binds to one of them.
Double description: these dictates are "but Conclusions, or Theoremes" (Lev. 15.41), yet considered as God's word they are properly laws. Open: which source obliges (divine command, prudence, reciprocity).

column1: State Hobbes's definition of liberty and say what it counts as free (Lev. 21.1–4).
column2:
Liberty, or FREEDOME, signifieth (properly) the absence of Opposition; (by Opposition, I mean externall Impediments of motion;) (Lev. 21.1). It applies to inanimate things as well as rational ones, and to bodies only; applied to anything else it is abused.
Consequences: "Feare and Liberty are consistent" (Lev. 21.3), so an act done from fear is free; liberty and necessity are consistent, as with water descending a channel (Lev. 21.4).
It also fixes who counts as free: a man who is not hindered from doing what he has a will to do.

column1: Distinguish contract, covenant and gift, and say which rights cannot be transferred (Lev. 14.9–13, 14.30).
column2:
The mutuall transferring of Right, is that which men call CONTRACT (Lev. 14.10). If one party performs now and the other is trusted to perform later, the trusted side is a pact or covenant; a one-sided transfer is a free gift.
Obligation is self-imposed: it arises only from one's own act of laying down a right.
Inalienable right: since "of the voluntary acts of every man, the object is some Good To Himselfe" (Lev. 14.9), no one can give up the right to resist force against his life: "A Covenant not to defend my selfe from force, by force, is alwayes voyd" (Lev. 14.30).

column1: Define justice and injustice in Hobbes and say when they begin (Lev. 15.1–3).
column2:
The third law of nature is "That Men Performe Their Covenants Made" (Lev. 15.1). Justice is defined by covenant: "the definition of INJUSTICE, is no other than The Not Performance Of Covenant. And whatsoever is not Unjust, is Just" (Lev. 15.2).
Covenants of mutual trust are void without a power to enforce them, so injustice can exist only once the cause of fear is removed, which requires a commonwealth.
So justice begins with the state, not because the sovereign decides by fiat what is just, but because there are no valid covenants to break until performance is secured (compare "Where there is no common Power, there is no Law: where no Law, no Injustice", Lev. 13.13).

column1: Who is the Fool, and what exactly does he deny (Lev. 15.4–5)?
column2:
He "hath sayd in his heart, there is no such thing as Justice" (Lev. 15.4), echoing Psalm 14. He does not deny that covenants exist, or that breaking them is called injustice; he denies that breaking them is always against reason, since it may conduce "to ones benefit" (Lev. 15.4).
The case is the second performer: the other side has performed, or a power compels both. Not the first-performer problem of the state of nature.
Hobbes's reply: breach is a bet on others' errors, since a breaker cannot be received into a society for defense except by their mistake (Lev. 15.5, paraphrased). Whether it works against a secret breaker is open (Hume's knave; Kavka, Gauthier, Hoekstra).

column1: Explain diffidence and anticipation as the engine of the state of war (Lev. 13.3–4).
column2:
Diffidence is distrust, not shyness. Anyone with something worth taking expects others to come prepared to dispossess him, so "there is no way for any man to secure himselfe, so reasonable, as Anticipation" (Lev. 13.4): master by force or wiles all you can.
Why the moderate join in: some take pleasure in conquest, and as long as one does and no one can tell who, even a moderate person's best defense is to strike first.
It is the second of the three causes of quarrel (competition, diffidence, glory), which make men invade for gain, safety and reputation.

column1: What is war in Hobbes's technical sense, and what does the condition lack (Lev. 13.8–13)?
column2:
War is a known disposition, not constant fighting: "the nature of War, consisteth not in actuall fighting; but in the known disposition thereto" (Lev. 13.8), as foul weather is not a shower or two.
It lacks industry, agriculture, navigation, building, knowledge, arts, letters and society, and has "continuall feare, and danger of violent death" (Lev. 13.9).
Evidence is by experience (America, civil war, sovereigns as gladiators), not as a history: the condition was "never generally so, over all the world" (Lev. 13.11).
Also: "Where there is no common Power, there is no Law: where no Law, no Injustice" (Lev. 13.13).

column1: Define person, author and actor, and explain how a multitude becomes one person (Lev. 16).
column2:
A person is one "whose words or actions are considered, either as his own, or as representing the words or actions of an other man" (Lev. 16.1). A natural person speaks for himself; an artificial one represents another.
Where the represented owns the words: "the Person is the Actor; and he that owneth his words and actions, is the AUTHOR: In which case the Actor acteth by Authority" (Lev. 16.4).
Key move: "it is the Unity of the Representer, not the Unity of the Represented, that maketh the Person One" (Lev. 16.13). There is no people with a will of its own apart from its representative.

column1: Define the commonwealth and the sovereign, and say what "Mortall God" means (Lev. 17).
column2:
The covenant: "I Authorise and give up my Right of Governing my selfe, to this Man, or to this Assembly of men, on this condition, that thou give up thy Right to him, and Authorise all his Actions in like manner" (Lev. 17.13).
The commonwealth is "One Person, of whose Acts a great Multitude, by mutuall Covenants one with another, have made themselves every one the Author" (Lev. 17.14); the bearer is the sovereign, everyone else a subject.
It is "that Mortall God, to which wee owe under the Immortall God, our peace and defence" (Lev. 17.13). The covenant is among the subjects only, so the sovereign makes no promise and cannot breach one.

column1: Distinguish a sovereign by institution from a sovereign by acquisition (Lev. 17, 20).
column2:
By institution: people covenant with one another to authorize a man or assembly, out of fear of one another. By acquisition: "men singly, or many together by plurality of voyces, for fear of death, or bonds, do authorise all the actions of that Man, or Assembly, that hath their lives and liberty in his Power" (Lev. 20).
Difference: they subject themselves to the one they fear. In both cases they act from fear, and "the Rights, and Consequences of Soveraignty, are the same in both" (Lev. 20).
The right comes from the vanquished's covenant, not from victory (Argument 13). A chained captive owes nothing.

column1: Distinguish iniquity from injury in Hobbes, and say why the sovereign cannot do the second (Lev. 18).
column2:
Each subject is author of the sovereign's acts, so "whatsoever he doth, it can be no injury to any of his Subjects" (Lev. 18), since no one can injure himself; a subject who complains of the sovereign complains of what he authored.
The sovereign may commit "Iniquity; but not Injustice, or Injury in the proper signification" (Lev. 18): he can act against the laws of nature and answer to God for it, but cannot wrong a subject in the covenant sense.
Caution: this is not a claim that subjects must like it; resistance rights (Lev. 21) remain for life and body.

column1: What is the liberty of subjects, and how does it differ from the true liberties (Lev. 21.5–21)?
column2:
Civil laws are "Artificiall Chains", fastened at one end to the lips of the sovereign and at the other to the subjects' own ears (Lev. 21.5). The liberty of subjects is what the chains leave free: "As for other Lyberties, they depend on the silence of the Law" (Lev. 21.18); it is consistent with unlimited sovereign power.
True liberties are the rights no covenant could transfer: a man ordered to harm himself "yet hath that man the Liberty to disobey" (Lev. 21.12). No one may resist the sovereign's sword to defend another (Lev. 21.17).
Limit: "The Obligation of Subjects to the Soveraign is understood to last as long, and no longer, than the power lasteth, by which he is able to protect them" (Lev. 21.21).

column1: Distinguish counsel from command, and say where the laws of nature fall (Lev. 25.2–3; 26).
column2:
Command is an order given "without expecting other reason than the Will of him that sayes it" (Lev. 25.2): it aims at the commander's good. Counsel gives reasons "from the benefit that arriveth by it to him to whom he saith it" (Lev. 25.3): it aims at the hearer's good.
Civil law is a command: the rules the commonwealth has commanded, by word, writing or other sufficient sign of the will; the sovereign is sole legislator.
The laws of nature, as theorems, are counsel; they become law as commands of God or of the sovereign. In a commonwealth "The Law of Nature, and the Civill Law, contain each other, and are of equall extent" (Lev. 26.8). Open: legal positivist or natural-law thinker?

column1: What are the natural seeds of religion, and how does Hobbes treat religion in Part I (Lev. 6.36; 12)?
column2:
Definition: "Feare of power invisible, feigned by the mind, or imagined from tales publiquely allowed, RELIGION; not allowed, superstition" (Lev. 6.36). Public allowance is built into the definition.
Natural seed: "Opinion of Ghosts, Ignorance of second causes, Devotion towards what men fear, and Taking of things Casuall for Prognostiques" (Lev. 12).
Founders and lawgivers cultivated the seeds to make people obedient, so "the Religion of the former sort, is a part of humane Politiques" (Lev. 12). Religion is thus a political force, dangerous in hands other than the sovereign's.

column1: What is the kingdom of darkness in Hobbes (Lev. 44-47)?
column2:
A confederacy of deceivers who, by misreading Scripture, mixing in pagan demonology and vain philosophy (scholastic Aristotelianism, with its separated essences and incorporeal substances), win dominion over people in this world (Lev. 44-46, paraphrased).
The Papacy is "no other, than the Ghost of the deceased Romane Empire, sitting crowned upon the grave thereof" (Lev. 47).
Function: Part IV applies the argument that a ghostly authority set against the civil one is a disease of the commonwealth. Open: sincere Christian (Martinich) or covert atheist (Curley, Jesseph)?

column1: State what the book says its purpose is, and how that connects to when obedience ends (Review and Conclusion; Lev. 21.21).
column2:
The last paragraph calls the work a "Discourse of Civill and Ecclesiasticall Government, occasioned by the disorders of the present time", written "to set before mens eyes the mutuall Relation between Protection and Obedience" (Review and Conclusion).
The same relation sets the limit: obedience lasts as long as the sovereign's power to protect (Lev. 21.21), so a subject of a defeated sovereign may submit to the victor once he has the liberty to do so.
Scholars dispute whether this is a de facto turn in 1651 (Skinner, Hoekstra) or continuous with De Cive.
